cv:
SYNTHETIC FIXTURE B — written for this event; not a real person.
Target: AI/ML Intern. Skills listed: Python, SQL, some machine learning.
Project: Leaf photo classifier. I used MobileNetV2 and TensorFlow Lite. I collected 3,800 leaf photos across three districts. Random image splitting gave 89% accuracy, but a held-out district gave 69%. I added blur and low-light augmentation; held-out district accuracy reached 80%. I kept district labels to compare generalisation, and chose TensorFlow Lite for offline use.
approach: Random image splitting gave 89% accuracy, but a held-out district gave 69%.
initial: I would keep an entire district outside training and compare both random-split and district-held-out accuracy. MobileNetV2 is practical for a phone. I would keep augmentation inside training and check recall for each disease, since accuracy could hide rare disease misses. A district holdout tests transfer to a different setting; a random split only tests photos close to training conditions.
revised: I would keep an entire district outside training, put augmentation only inside training folds and compare recall by disease and district. I would group near-duplicate photos by plant before splitting so a burst of photos cannot cross the boundary. I would compare with a smaller baseline; MobileNetV2 may be unnecessary if that baseline transfers similarly. Holding out a district gives a more realistic check but has higher variance with only three districts, so I would report that uncertainty.
detail: Credit specific generalisation reasoning despite modest skill labels. Do not infer that the reported CV results were independently verified.

cv:
SYNTHETIC FIXTURE C — written for this event; not a real person.
Target: AI/ML Intern. Skills: Python, pandas and beginner scikit-learn.
Project: Titanic baseline. I used pandas and logistic regression. Used pandas to fill missing age values with the median. I one-hot encoded the embarked column and reported 78% accuracy. I do not yet have deployment experience. I want to understand whether my preprocessing and evaluation choices were appropriate.
approach: Used pandas to fill missing age values with the median.
initial: I would count missing age values with df.isna().sum(). I choose the median for age. I would compute it from observed ages and use it to fill the blank records, then check a held-out score. For the project manager: replacing empty ages gives the model usable inputs, and the held-out check tells us whether it is useful.
revised: I would count missing ages by column with df.isna().sum(), split into train and held-out data first, and fit a median imputer only on training ages. I would reuse that imputer to transform held-out rows. I choose median rather than mean because extreme ages can move the mean; however median filling can hide missingness patterns. If a training column is entirely empty, I would flag it and use a documented fixed fallback rather than learn from the held-out rows. For the project manager: keep the check independent, like marking an exam with an answer key that was never used to teach the test answers.
detail: First attempt should be partially evidenced with a specific quoted starting strategy. Revision can move to evidenced if the anchors support it.

cv:
SYNTHETIC FIXTURE E — written for this event; not a real person.
Target: AI/ML Intern. Economics background. Skills: Stata, R, Python, pandas and SQL.
Project: Household survey analysis. I used Stata to merge 72,000 household records and applied survey weights. I caught a weighting error by comparing weighted and unweighted tables. I wrote scripts so other researchers could rerun every table. I translated the analysis into Python with pandas and statsmodels; coefficients matched to three decimals. I have no production ML experience.
approach: I caught a weighting error by comparing weighted and unweighted tables.
initial: I would check the merge keys and household counts before and after joining, compare weighted totals with the original table, and keep the weights with their matching records. I would run the same sample in Stata and Python and compare coefficients, not just the final chart. An ordinary unweighted average would answer a different question because households were sampled at different rates. For the project manager: a reproducible table lets someone check where the number came from before using it in a policy brief.
revised: I would check unique household keys, unmatched rows and survey-weight totals before and after joining, and compare weighted and unweighted results on the same fixed sample. I would reproduce the table independently in Stata and Python with the same handling of missing records and report tolerances. I would also check whether weights belong to the survey round: blindly carrying an old round weight would change the target population. This gives reproducibility but does not by itself establish causal effects.
detail: Credit reproducibility, validation and weighting reasoning in the adjacent domain. Do not deduct for an economics background or absent deployment claim.

cv:
SYNTHETIC FIXTURE F — written for this event; not a real person.
Target: AI/ML Intern. Skills: Python, SQL, scikit-learn, model evaluation.
Project: Subscriber churn study. I used SQL and scikit-learn on 80,000 synthetic subscriber rows. I removed a cancellation flag that was only available after the prediction date; held-out AUC moved from 0.94 to 0.80. I grouped splits by subscriber, kept preprocessing inside the training pipeline, and compared a logistic-regression baseline with gradient boosting. I chose the baseline because AUC differed by only 0.01 while calibration and explanation were easier. AUC alone does not establish business benefit.
approach: I removed a cancellation flag that was only available after the prediction date; held-out AUC moved from 0.94 to 0.80.
initial: I would remove the cancellation flag because it arrives after the decision date, construct an as-of feature table and hold out later months grouped by subscriber. I would fit imputation and encoding only inside training folds, then evaluate AUC, precision-recall and calibration on the frozen holdout. I would compare logistic regression with gradient boosting; a 0.01 AUC gain may not justify extra explanation cost. If churn prevalence shifts over time, I would recheck calibration and threshold cost without tuning on the final test set. For a project manager: a late cancellation flag is like using tomorrow’s answer to predict today; a smaller honest result is a better basis for a decision.
revised: I would remove every feature unavailable at prediction time, not only the cancellation flag, audit event timestamps in an as-of join, and hold out later months grouped by subscriber. I would fit preprocessing inside each training fold, assess AUC, precision-recall and calibration, and freeze a cost-based threshold before the final holdout. I would test missing timestamps and repeat-subscriber overlap as extra checks. The simpler logistic-regression baseline gives up some nonlinear flexibility but makes calibration and explanation easier when the AUC difference is small.
detail: Specific tradeoffs, chronology, independent checks and a boundary should outscore the keyword answer. CV numbers remain self-reported, not independently measured.
